translation: Two other small photos with scalloped edges, likely from the same year, show the same child, but smaller, in a dress with ruffles and puff sleeves.
In the first one, she snuggles mischievously against a woman with a large body, all in one piece in a wide-striped dress, her hair piled up in big rolls.
In the other, she raises her left fist, her right is held back by the hand of a tall man, in a light jacket and pleated trousers, with a nonchalant posture.
The two photos were taken on the same day in front of a low wall topped with a border of flowers, in a cobblestone courtyard.
Above their heads passes a clothesline, on which a peg has remained attached.

Another photo, signed by the same photographer but the booklet paper is more ordinary and the gold trim has disappeared presumably destined for the same family distribution, shows a little girl of about four years old, serious, almost sad despite a cute chubby face under short hair, parted in the middle and pulled back by clips to which ribbons are attached, like butterflies.
The left hand rests on the same fully visible, Louis XVI style carved table.
She appears pudgy in her bodice, her skirt hitched up at the front due to a prominent belly, possibly a sign of rickets (around 1944).
The boys were proud to join the regiment and they looked handsome in their soldier's uniforms.
On the evening of the military review, they went from café to café celebrating their recognition as real men.
Before the regiment, they were still children and of no worth in the job market or marriage market.
Afterwards, they could have a wife and children.
The uniform they paraded around the neighborhood during leave draped them in patriotic beauty and virtual sacrifice.
The shadow of the victorious fighters, the GIs, hovered around them.
The coarse cloth of the tunic, brushed against when one stood on tiptoe to kiss them, symbolized the absolute division between the world of men and that of women.
Seeing them elicited a feeling of heroism.

Under the unchanging, the posters of last year's circus with the photo of Roger Lanzac, the first communion pictures distributed to friends, the Chansonniers Club on Radio Luxembourg, the days were filled with new desires.
On Sunday afternoons, people would crowd around the general electrical shop's storefront to watch the television.
Cafes were investing in buying a station to attract customers.
On the sides of the hills, motocross tracks wound their way and one could watch deafening machines going up and down all day long.
The growing impatience of commerce with its new watchwords, "initiative", "dynamism", was shaking up the routine of the cities.
Between the funfair and the fair, the Commercial Fortnight was setting up as a spring ritual.
In the downtown streets, loudspeakers blared out encouragements to buy, interspersed with songs by Annie Cordy and Eddie Constantine, all to win the Simca or the dining room set.

On the podium, in the town hall square, a local presenter was making people laugh with jokes from Roger Nicolas and Jean Richard, drumming up candidates for the Hook or Double or Quit, just like on the radio.
Seated in a corner of the podium, the Queen of Commerce reigned under her crown.
The merchandise advanced under the colors of the festival.
People would say "it's a change" or "one mustn't get stuck in a rut, it's mind-numbing to stay at home".
But they only spoke of what they had seen, which could be relived by eating and drinking.
They lacked the talent or conviction to talk about what they knew but had not seen.
So, neither Jewish children boarding trains for Auschwitz, nor starving people collected in the morning in the Warsaw ghetto, nor 10,000 degrees at Hiroshima.

Hence this impression that history lessons, documentaries, and films, later on, would not dissipate: neither the crematorium ovens nor the atomic bomb were in the same era as black market butter, air raid warnings and trips to the basement.
By comparison, they switched on to the previous war, the Great One, that of '14, won in blood and glory, a man's war which the women at the table listened to with respect.
They were talking about the Chemin des Dames and Verdun, about those gassed, about the bells of November 11th, 1918.
They named villages from which not a single child who had gone to the front had returned.
They contrasted the soldiers in the muddy trenches with the prisoners of '40 who stayed warm and safe for five years without even having bombs dropped on their heads.
They were arguing over heroism and misfortune.

The children weren't listening and hurried to leave the table as soon as they had been given permission, taking advantage of the general good will on holidays to engage in forbidden games, jumping on the beds and swinging upside down.
But they held everything back.

Next to the fabulous times of which they wouldn't order the episodes for a long time, the Debacle, the Exodus, the Occupation, the Landing, Victory they found dull that nameless one in which they were growing up.
They regretted not having been born, or barely, when it was time to depart in a cohort on the roads and sleep on straw like gypsies.
They would keep a tenacious regret for this unfulfilled time.
The memories of others passed on to them a secret nostalgia for this era that they had barely missed and the hope to live it one day.
The frenzy that followed the Liberation was fading.
Then people could only think about going out and the world was full of desires to be satisfied immediately.
Everything that was a first since the war caused a rush, the bananas, the national lottery tickets, the fireworks.

By entire neighborhoods, from the grandmother supported by her daughters to the infant in a pram, people rushed to the fair, to the torchlight procession, to the Bouglione circus where they almost got trampled in the stampede.
They gathered in a praying and singing crowd on the road to welcome the statue of Our Lady of Boulogne and escort it for miles the next day.
Secular or religious, any occasion was a good one for them to be outside together, as if they wanted to continue living collectively.
On Sunday evenings, the buses would return from the sea carrying tall young men in shorts who were singing loudly on the luggage rack.
The dogs roamed freely and mated in the middle of the street.
Family stories and social narratives are one and the same.

The voices of the guests defined the realms of youth: the countryside and farms where, from time immemorial, men had been hired and girls had served, the factory where everyone had met, socialized and married, and the small businesses to which the most ambitious had ascended.

They drew pictures of lives with no personal incidents other than births, marriages and bereavements, without journeys beyond the garrison town in the distance, lives filled with work, its hardness and weariness, threats from drinking.
The school was a mythical backdrop, a brief golden age where the teacher had been the harsh god with his iron ruler for slapping fingers.
From hand to hand passed photos, browned and stained on the back by all the fingers that had held them during other meals, a blend of coffee and grease fused into an indefinable color.
In the solemn and stiff newlyweds, the wedding guests arrayed in several rows along a wall, one could not recognize either one's relatives or anyone else.
It was not oneself one saw in the half-naked, gender-indistinct baby on a cushion but someone else, a creature belonging to a mute and inaccessible time.
